prompt: Can you make a one-page site for Kilnfolk, a two-person pottery studio that sells glazed stoneware mugs and bowls in small monthly drops? I need a hero, three featured pieces with prices, a short about, and a newsletter signup. They want it to feel handmade and warm but not twee. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets.
rubric: Headings and body are visibly different typefaces or a clearly different treatment, and the warmth comes from a considered system-font choice (for example an old-style or humanist serif stack) rather than a script, novelty or default-looking face.
Every font-family declaration is a real stack that names several system faces for different platforms and ends in a generic family; nothing relies on a downloaded font, @import or link tag.
Body copy renders at a comfortable reading size with a measured line length and generous leading, not small grey text running the full window width.
No more than two type families appear on the page, and the prices read as clean figures that line up across the three pieces.
The page does not fake handmade character with decorative or cursive fonts for long text.

prompt: We run the Harbor Line passenger ferry and need a page riders see when sailings are delayed. Banner at the top saying what's going on, then a table of the next six departures with the time, the boat name and a status (on time, delayed 15 min, cancelled), and the terminal phone number at the bottom. People will mostly be reading it on their phones standing on the dock in bright sun. Single HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Departure times and delay minutes line up in their columns (tabular figures, a monospaced treatment for the numerals, or equivalent), so rows scan vertically.
Text is set at a size and weight that suits bright-sun phone reading: body not below about 16px, no hairline or very light weights, status text clearly legible.
Status is carried by a legible word and a visible typographic difference (weight, case or size), not by colour alone.
The font stack is a functional system UI stack with named platform fallbacks and a generic family, and the page uses one family or at most a clear sans plus a restrained second for numerals.
The phone number is set large enough to read and tap, and its digits are unambiguous.

prompt: I do communications for a small legal aid nonprofit. We publish 15 to 30 page guides for tenants (evictions, repairs, deposits) as web pages and as printed handouts. A lot of our readers use older Android phones or the library computers. We have basically no budget. What typefaces should we use for the guides?
rubric: Recommends a concrete body typeface or stack suited to long reading on modest screens, not a display or decorative face, and says why in terms of the readers' devices.
Keeps to zero-cost options and is accurate about licensing, such as system fonts or openly licensed families, and does not suggest a paid font.
Covers both the web and the printed handout, saying whether the same family can serve both.
Gives a fallback stack that ends in a generic family and is honest about which faces can't be assumed on older Android or library Windows machines.
Names what to check on real devices (an old phone, a library computer, a test print) instead of claiming the choice is guaranteed to look right.
Identifies that five or six unrelated families with many weights is the main cause of the chaotic feel and recommends cutting to one or two families with a few weights.
Calls out that body text is set in a script face at 13px with tight leading and that this hurts reading, and moves body to a plain readable face.
Flags the very thin weights (100 to 200) at small sizes as hard to read.
Points to the render-blocking @import, the number of weights downloaded, and display=block as reasons for slowness or invisible text, and that most families have no real fallback stack.
Offers a concrete replacement setup that still keeps some of the friendly personality for a children's practice rather than flattening it to corporate.

prompt: Our designer says the site looks crisp and light on her MacBook. On my Windows office monitor and my dad's old Android tablet the same text looks thinner and kind of jagged. It's the same CSS and the same font files. Why would that happen, and what should we do about it?
rubric: Explains that platforms and screens render the same font differently (anti-aliasing, hinting, pixel density), so it is not necessarily a CSS bug.
Says that light weights and small sizes suffer most on low-density Windows and Android screens and suggests concrete adjustments such as a heavier weight or slightly larger size for body text.
Does not promise a single CSS property that makes Windows match the Mac, and is honest about what cannot be controlled.
Says what to test on: real Windows at 100% scaling, a low-density screen and an older Android device, rather than only a high-density Mac.
Stays at a length and tone a non-specialist can follow.
Says plainly near the start that the setup is already sound and why (system stack with fallbacks, readable size and leading, tabular figures, monospace for code).
Leaves the stacks, sizes and structure essentially as they are; any change is small and explained (for example noting that weight 650 may snap to 600 or 700 on non-variable system fonts).
Does not introduce a web font, a display face or a second family, and does not rewrite the file wholesale.
Frames any optional extra as optional and does not invent problems to have something to fix.

prompt: Quick one, two sentences max please: I'm building a recipe app as an offline-capable PWA. What should the CSS font-family be?
rubric: The whole answer is at most two sentences, with no headings, bullets or preamble.
Gives a usable font-family value that ends in a generic family.
The choice is tied to offline use (system fonts, or a font that is bundled and cached) rather than a remote font service.
Does not ask clarifying questions instead of answering.

prompt: Our brand designer gave us the logo files and said our brand typeface is "Marlowe Grotesk". She installed the .otf files on all our laptops. I'd like to just upload those files to our website and load them with @font-face. Is that fine? And what should the fallback be so the site looks okay until we sort it?
rubric: Does not simply say yes: points out that a licence for installing fonts on computers often does not cover web embedding, and that this needs to be checked.
Says who to ask or what to look for (the designer, the foundry, the licence document) and does not claim to know the actual terms of this particular font.
Gives a practical interim fallback stack of widely available sans-serif system faces ending in a generic family, with a note that it will not match the brand font exactly.
Mentions that a web-ready format and a webfont licence are the usual route if the licence allows it, without a long lecture.

prompt: We're building a small savings-group app for market vendors. Most of them have mid-range Android phones on prepaid data and the app has to work with spotty or no connection. The founder wants it to look "friendly and modern". Which fonts should we use?
rubric: Keeps the font payload very small: recommends system fonts or at most one small, subsetted file, and ties this to prepaid data and offline use.
Gives a stack that does not assume a particular Android font is present and ends in a generic family.
Gets "friendly and modern" through available means (weight, size, rounded system choices, spacing) without requiring a heavy downloaded face.
Says that the languages and scripts the vendors read decide whether a face is adequate, and asks or flags this rather than assuming Latin only.
Sets amounts in a way that lines up (tabular figures) or at least mentions money figures need to be readable at a glance.

prompt: We're redoing the notice for a city bus route change. It has to be in Hindi and English. It has route numbers, stop names and the new times. It will be printed at A3 and also sent as a PDF that people open on their phones. How should I handle the type? What gets bigger, and what do I do about the two scripts?
rubric: Sets up a clear order of roles with concrete relationships (route number largest, then stop names, then times and secondary text) rather than vague advice.

Addresses pairing a Devanagari-capable typeface with a Latin one so weight and apparent size match, and notes that Devanagari usually needs more size and line height than Latin at the same point size.
Warns that a Latin-only font will not render Hindi and cause missing glyphs or a silent fallback, and says to pick faces that cover both scripts.
Treats times as figures that need to be unambiguous and aligned, and says how to handle numerals in the two scripts consistently.
Says to check the PDF with fonts embedded and to test a proof print and the phone view.
